name: Recoletos
etymology_summary: Named after the Convento de Recoletos de San Agustin, a convent of Augustinian Recollects (reformed Augustinians) founded in 1592 and demolished in 1836. The Paseo de Recoletos preserves the memory.
named_after: Convento de Recoletos de San Agustin

name: Sol
etymology_summary: From the Puerta del Sol, an east-facing gate in Madrid's medieval wall decorated with a sun motif. First documented in 15th century records.

name: Atocha
etymology_summary: From 'atocha' (esparto grass, Stipa tenacissima) that grew abundantly in the area. First documented in the Fuero de Madrid (1202) as 'Prato de Toia'. Spain's first railway terminus (Madrid-Aranjuez, 1851).

name: Chamartin-Clara Campoamor
etymology_summary: Chamartin: from the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa, annexed 1948. Etymology debated: possibly Basque 'ecta-Martin' (village of captain Martin) per Menendez Pidal, or French 'Chez Martin'. Clara Campoamor (1888-1972): feminist politician who achieved women's suffrage in Spain in 1931.

name: Nuevos Ministerios
etymology_summary: Named after the government ministry buildings ('Nuevos Ministerios') built 1933-1942 on the former hippodrome site, designed by Secundino Zuazo under commission from Indalecio Prieto.

name: Fuente de la Mora
etymology_summary: Named after the old Camino Fuente de la Mora road. 'Fuente' means spring/fountain; 'Mora' may derive from pre-Roman root 'mor-' meaning heap of stones, suggesting 'spring among the rocks'. Originally planned as 'Manoteras'.

name: Aeropuerto T4
etymology_summary: Named for its location at Terminal 4 of Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas Airport. The airport itself is named after the first elected PM of democratic Spain.

name: Principe Pio
etymology_summary: Named after the Montana del Principe Pio (now Parque de la Montana). Francisco Pio de Saboya y Moura (1659-1726) was an Italian aristocrat and supporter of Felipe V. The station was originally called 'Estacion del Norte' (1861).

name: Mendez Alvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Francisco Mendez Alvaro (1806-1883), physician, hygienist, and pioneer of public health in Madrid. The street was formerly called Calle del Sur.

name: Delicias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Delicias ('Promenade of Delights'), an 18th-century tree-lined boulevard created under Fernando VI leading to the Manzanares river. The first permanent railway station in Madrid was built here in 1880.

name: Piramides
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Piramides, which takes its name from two 14m obelisks built in 1831 by Francisco Javier de Marietegui. Despite the name, they are actually obelisks not pyramids.

name: Embajadores
etymology_summary: Named after the street and area. In 1435, during a plague outbreak, King Juan II sent French ambassadors ('embajadores') to an area outside the city walls. The zone became known as 'Campo de Embajadores'.

name: Doce de Octubre
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, inaugurated on October 12, 1973. The hospital's name commemorates the Spanish national holiday (Dia de la Hispanidad).

name: Orcasitas
etymology_summary: Named after the Orcasitas neighbourhood, which took its name from the Orcasitas family who owned the farmland where the neighbourhood developed in the 1940s.

name: Puente Alcocer
etymology_summary: Named after a bridge ('puente') in the Villaverde Alto area. 'Alcocer' likely derives from Arabic 'al-qusayr' (small palace/fortress).

name: San Cristobal de los Angeles
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood. 'San Cristobal' refers to St. Christopher; 'de los Angeles' refers to proximity to the Cerro de los Angeles, the geographic centre of the Iberian Peninsula. Station opened 1851 on original Madrid-Aranjuez line.

name: San Cristobal Industrial
etymology_summary: Extension of the San Cristobal de los Angeles name, with 'Industrial' added to denote the adjacent industrial zone.

name: Getafe Industrial
etymology_summary: Named after the industrial zone of Getafe. Originally called 'Getafe-Alicante'. Located near the Getafe Air Base and Airbus manufacturing facility.

name: Getafe Centro
etymology_summary: Named for its location in central Getafe. The city name derives from Arabic 'Xatafi' (from 'Jata', meaning 'long'), referring to its long main street along the royal road between Madrid and Toledo.

name: Getafe Sector 3
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Sector 3' neighbourhood of Getafe, a planned residential development. Opened 1995.

name: Las Margaritas Universidad
etymology_summary: 'Las Margaritas' is a 1960s neighbourhood in Getafe with flower-themed street names (Lilas, Loto, Camelias). 'Universidad' refers to Carlos III University campus nearby.

name: El Casar
etymology_summary: Named after the El Casar area of Getafe Norte. 'Casar' derives from Latin 'casale' meaning a group of houses or a hamlet.

name: Pinto
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Latin 'punctum' (point/crossing), as Pinto was a crossroads of Roman roads and considered the geographic centre of the Iberian Peninsula. Alternative Arabic legend theory also exists.

name: Valdemoro
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Most likely from 'Val de Moro' (Valley of the Moor), named after the Reconquista. Alternative theories: Arabic 'Wadi al-murr' (bitter river) or pre-Roman 'mor-' (stones). First documented as 'Vallem Maurii' under Alfonso VIII.

name: Ciempozuelos
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'cien pozuelos' (a hundred small wells), referring to the many wells dug to access groundwater. 'Cien' is not literal but means 'many'. Roman settlement may have been called Ischadia ('land of fig trees').

name: Aranjuez
etymology_summary: Named after the royal town. Etymology debated: possibly from Basque 'arantza' (thorns), pre-Roman root '*aranz' (stream), or Latin 'Ara Jovis' (altar of Jupiter). Documented as 'Aranz' in 13th century. Terminus of Spain's first railway (1851).

name: Parla
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Etymology debated: possibly from Roman anthroponym 'Parilus', from Latin 'parabola' (speech), or from 'palus' (swamp). Popular legend: a mute woman drank from a local fountain and began to 'parlar' (speak).

name: Fuencarral
etymology_summary: Named after the former municipality (annexed 1951). From 'fuente carra' (fountain where carts stop): a fountain where the carters' animals drank. 'Carra' refers to the stopping area for carts.

name: Cantoblanco Universidad
etymology_summary: 'Cantoblanco' likely means 'white rock/edge' (from 'canto' = stone/edge + 'blanco' = white), describing the terrain. 'Universidad' refers to the Universidad Autonoma de Madrid campus located here since 1970.

name: Alcobendas-San Sebastian de los Reyes
etymology_summary: Named after both municipalities. 'Alcobendas': pre-Roman origin, possibly 'Alcevindos' (hill of the deer) per Francisco Villar. First documented in Fuero de Madrid (1202). 'San Sebastian de los Reyes': from the ermita of San Sebastian and protection of the Reyes Catolicos (1492).

name: El Goloso
etymology_summary: Named after the El Goloso neighbourhood, which itself is named after the military base established there in the early 20th century.

name: Colmenar Viejo
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'colmenar' (apiary/place of beehives) + 'viejo' (old). According to Felipe II's 1579 surveys, the town grew around an old beekeeper's house along the Alcala-Segovia road. First documented 1287.

name: Asamblea de Madrid-Entrevias
etymology_summary: Originally named 'Entrevias' (1977), meaning 'between the tracks', as the neighbourhood is surrounded by railway lines. Renamed in 1998 when the Asamblea de Madrid (regional parliament) building opened nearby.

name: El Pozo
etymology_summary: Named after the 'Pozo del Tio Raimundo' neighbourhood. According to tradition, a farmer named Raimundo built a well ('pozo') and watering trough for passing livestock.

name: Santa Eugenia
etymology_summary: Named after the Santa Eugenia neighbourhood (1970s planned development). Streets are named after towns in Burgos province, reflecting the origin of the developers. The saint's name was likely chosen arbitrarily for the development.

name: Coslada
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Etymology debated: possibly from Latin 'cos' (flint) + 'late' (abundant), meaning 'place of abundant flint'; or from Celtic 'cosla' (hazelnut), meaning 'hazelnut grove'; or from Latin 'cova ustulata' (burnt cave).

name: San Fernando
etymology_summary: Named after San Fernando de Henares. The municipality was named in honour of King Fernando VI, who developed a royal textile factory there from 1746. 'De Henares' refers to the nearby river.

name: Torrejon de Ardoz
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Torrejon' from Latin 'turris' (tower), diminutive chain 'torre > torreja > torrejon', referring to a medieval watchtower. 'Ardoz' is a hydronym from the Arroyo Ardoz stream.

name: Soto del Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the residential neighbourhood built along the Henares river. 'Soto' means a wooded riverside area or grove, common in Castilian toponymy.

name: La Garena
etymology_summary: Named after the La Garena residential neighbourhood in Alcala de Henares. The etymology of 'garena' is uncertain but may relate to an old property or agricultural plot name.

name: Alcala de Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the city. 'Alcala' from Arabic 'al-qala' (the fortress), referring to the citadel of Qal'at Abd al-Salam. 'De Henares' from the river, possibly from Latin 'foenarius' or Arabic 'en-Nahr'. Roman name was Complutum ('confluence').

name: Alcala de Henares Universidad
etymology_summary: Named for proximity to the historic University of Alcala, founded by Cardinal Cisneros in 1499. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1998.

name: Meco
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Etymology debated: possibly Celtic 'miccon' (sheep), Roman 'miaccum' (country house), or Arabic 'maksusk' (bare mountain).

name: Azuqueca
etymology_summary: Named after Azuqueca de Henares. From Arabic 'sukayqa' (diminutive of suq, 'little road/alley'), referring to a small path around which the first buildings were constructed.

name: Guadalajara
etymology_summary: Named after the city. From Arabic 'wad al-hayara' (valley of stones). The Arab city was founded 8th-9th century as 'madinat al-Faray' on the banks of the 'wad al-hayara' (the Henares river).

name: Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after the Aluche neighbourhood. Derives from the Arroyo Luche stream, a tributary of the Manzanares. Documented as 'Aluche' in a Real Cedula of Felipe II (1580). Alternative theory: from Leonese wrestling ('luches') brought by immigrants.

name: Maestra Justa Freire-Polideportivo Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after Justa Freire Mendez (1896-1965), innovative pedagogue and teacher. She pioneered progressive education methods in Madrid's working-class neighbourhoods. 'Polideportivo Aluche' refers to the adjacent sports complex.

name: Las Aguilas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Aguilas neighbourhood in the Latina district. The name likely refers to eagles that once inhabited the area or to the heraldic imagery associated with local estates.

name: Cuatro Vientos
etymology_summary: Named after the Cuatro Vientos area, which was already known by this name when Spain's first military aerodrome was established there in 1911. 'Four winds' likely describes the exposed, windy location on open terrain.

name: Laguna
etymology_summary: Named after the Laguna neighbourhood. 'Laguna' means 'lagoon' or 'small lake', suggesting historical presence of a body of standing water in the area.

name: Alcorcon
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Arabic 'al-kur' or 'alcor' (hill/mound). Originally an Arab watchtower on a hill to monitor Christian troop movements. Also linked to pottery tradition: 'alcor' was the paste for glazing clay.

name: San Jose de Valderas
etymology_summary: Named after the San Jose de Valderas neighbourhood of Alcorcon. 'San Jose' is St. Joseph; 'Valderas' likely from 'valle de eras' (valley of threshing floors). Station had origins on the old narrow-gauge Madrid-Almorox line.

name: Las Retamas
etymology_summary: Named after the avenue and the abundant retama (broom plant, Retama sphaerocarpa) bushes in the area. 'Retama' is from Arabic 'ratama'.

name: Mostoles
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Most accepted etymology: from Latin 'monisterium/monisteriis' (monasteries), indicating pre-Islamic Christian monasteries existed here. Alternative: from 'mustum et olea' (must and olive oil).

name: Mostoles-El Soto
etymology_summary: 'Mostoles' - see above. 'El Soto' means 'the grove', referring to a wooded riverside area. Combined name indicates the station serves the southern/river side of Mostoles.

name: Leganes
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'legamo/legano' (mud/silt). Founded 1280 under Alfonso X. Originally called 'Legamar' or 'Leganos', referring to the muddy, lagoon-filled terrain used for agriculture. First documented 1232.

name: Parque Polvoranca
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Polvoranca regional park in Leganes. 'Polvoranca' likely relates to 'polvo' (dust) or refers to an old gunpowder factory or dust-producing terrain.

name: Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'fuente labrada' (carved/hewn fountain). According to the municipal archive, an old stone-built fountain made by the Moors gave the settlement its name. Founded late 14th century.

name: La Serna-Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: 'La Serna' derives from Latin 'senara' (sown field), a term used in medieval Castile for cultivated land. 'Fuenlabrada' added to indicate the municipality.

name: Humanes
etymology_summary: Named after Humanes de Madrid. Possibly from Latin 'humidus' (humid/wet), describing the terrain. First documented in 1141 when Alfonso VII donated the villa to Pedro Brimonis.

name: Aravaca
etymology_summary: Named after the Aravaca district. Of Celtic origin per Caridad Arias (2004). Documented as a municipality since Alfonso VIII's fuero (1222). Annexed to Madrid in 1951.

name: El Barrial-Centro Comercial Pozuelo
etymology_summary: Originally named 'El Barrial' after the neighbourhood. 'Barrial' means a muddy/clay area. Later 'Centro Comercial Pozuelo' was added after the nearby Hipercor shopping centre opened.

name: Pozuelo
etymology_summary: Named after Pozuelo de Alarcon. 'Pozuelo' from 'pozo' (well), meaning 'place with wells/springs'. Originally 'Pozuelo de Aravaca'. In 1632 Gabriel Ocana de Alarcon bought the town and changed its name.

name: Majadahonda
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'majada' (sheepfold/livestock resting place) + 'honda' (deep/low-lying). Refers to a deep hollow where shepherds gathered livestock. Founded by Segovian herders in the 13th century.

name: Las Rozas
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'roza' (cleared land for first-time cultivation). The name indicates agricultural origins: land cleared for farming along the road from Segovia.

name: Pinar
etymology_summary: Named after 'Pinar de las Rozas' (Pine Grove of Las Rozas). Refers to the pine forest area in the municipality of Las Rozas. Full name is Pinar de las Rozas.

name: Las Matas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Matas neighbourhood of Las Rozas. 'Matas' means 'bushes' or 'shrubland', describing the natural vegetation of the area.

name: Torrelodones
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From 'torre' (tower) + 'lodones' (hackberry/nettle trees, Celtis australis). Refers to a medieval watchtower surrounded by lodon trees. First documented 1287.

name: Galapagar-La Navata
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality and neighbourhood. 'Galapagar' from 'galapago' (tortoise) + collective suffix '-ar', meaning 'place of tortoises'. Alternative: from 'calapacar' (calabash field). 'La Navata' is a neighbourhood.

name: San Yago
etymology_summary: Named after a local area in Galapagar. 'San Yago' is an archaic form of 'Santiago' (Saint James), the patron saint of Spain. Reflects medieval pilgrimage traditions.

name: El Escorial
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Etymology debated: Father Siguenza (16th c.) suggested Latin 'scoria' (slag/waste), but Sarmiento (18th c.) proposed 'esculus' (type of oak). Recent studies favour the oak forest theory.

name: Robledo de Chavela
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Robledo' from Latin 'roburetum' (oak grove). 'Chavela': debated - possibly 'cha-vela' (father Vela) from medieval Basque-Romance; or from Arabic 'Djebel' (mountain); or from Latin 'casa' + 'Vela' (Vela's estate).

name: Santa Maria de la Alameda-Peguerinos
etymology_summary: 'Santa Maria de la Alameda': named after a church dedicated to the Virgin Mary near a poplar grove ('alameda', from 'alamo' = poplar). 'Peguerinos' refers to the nearby village, from 'peguero' (pitch worker/tar maker).

name: Los Negrales
etymology_summary: Named after the Los Negrales residential area of Alpedrete, near Collado Villalba. 'Negrales' likely refers to dark-coloured rocks or dark vegetation in the area.

name: Alpedrete
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. Hybrid word: Arabic article 'al-' + Romance 'pedrete' (stony place). Literally 'the rocky place', referring to the abundant granite stone quarries.

name: Collado Mediano
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. 'Collado' means 'pass/col', a low point for crossing between hills; in medieval pastoral usage also 'livestock enclosure'. 'Mediano' means 'medium-sized', perhaps referring to a modestly sized corral.

name: Los Molinos
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. In 1546, Alvaro de Mena received a licence to build a water mill on the Guadarrama river, which gave the settlement its name 'Los Molinos' (The Mills).

name: Cercedilla
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality. From Latin 'quercetum' (oak grove), via diminutive form. 'Cercedilla' = 'little Cerceda'. The name was likely given by settlers from nearby Cerceda. Origin as a Roman road settlement on the Segovia-Titulcia route.

name: Puerto de Navacerrada
etymology_summary: Named after the mountain pass. 'Puerto' means 'mountain pass'. 'Navacerrada' from 'nava' (high plain/meadow) + 'cerrada' (enclosed). Station at 1765m altitude on the C-9 mountain railway.

name: Cotos
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerto de los Cotos mountain pass (1819m). 'Cotos' refers to boundary marker stones placed by Carlos III in 1761 when he purchased the Valsain lands and demarcated his territory.

name: Mirasierra-Paco de Lucia
etymology_summary: 'Mirasierra' means 'view of the mountains'. 'Paco de Lucia' honours Francisco Sanchez Gomez (1947-2014), the world-renowned flamenco guitarist who lived in this neighbourhood. Originally planned as 'Costa Brava'.

name: Ramon y Cajal
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Hospital Universitario Ramon y Cajal, which honours Santiago Ramon y Cajal (1852-1934), Nobel Prize-winning neuroscientist and 'father of modern neuroscience'.

name: Pitis
etymology_summary: Named after the Pitis area in Fuencarral-El Pardo district, a pre-existing rural place name documented well before the railway station opened in 1964. The exact origin is uncertain. One hypothesis links it to Greek 'Pitys' (pine), a nymph transformed into a pine tree, which would connect to the area's historical pine forests. A shantytown grew around the station until its demolition c. 2005.

name: Tres Cantos
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality (179th of Madrid region, independent since 1991). Most accepted theory: named after three large granite boulders ('cantos') that served as landmarks where livestock traders met. No definitive documentation exists.

name: Valdebebas
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdebebas area. The name refers to the Arroyo de Valdebebas, the last natural stream within Madrid city. 'Valde-' from 'valle de' (valley of); 'bebas' possibly from a personal name or pre-Roman root. The stream rises in Fuencarral and flows to the Jarama.

name: Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the Vallecas area. 'Vallecas' etymology debated: possibly from Latin 'vallis' + Arab name 'Kas' (Valley of Kas), or from 'Vallis Egas'. First documented in 1202. Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the Vicalvaro district. 'Vicalvaro' from Arabic 'Vicus Albari' (village of Albaro) or possibly 'vicus alvarus' (white village). Independent until annexed by Madrid in 1951. Famous for the 'Vicalvarada' (1854), a military uprising.

name: Villaverde Bajo
etymology_summary: Named after the Villaverde Bajo neighbourhood. 'Villaverde' = 'green village' from Latin 'villa viridis'. 'Bajo' = 'lower'. Villaverde was independent until annexed by Madrid in 1954.

name: Villaverde Alto
etymology_summary: Named after Villaverde Alto, the historic centre of the former municipality. 'Villaverde' = 'green village'. 'Alto' = 'upper/high'. Major railway junction point.

name: Universidad P. Comillas
etymology_summary: Named after the Universidad Pontificia Comillas campus. Founded 1890 in Comillas (Cantabria) by the 1st Marquis of Comillas, Antonio Lopez y Lopez. Moved to Madrid in 1960s. 'Comillas' from Latin 'cumella' (little hilltop).

name: Valdelasfuentes
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdelasfuentes area of Alcobendas. 'Valde las fuentes' = 'valley of the springs/fountains'. Describes the historically water-rich terrain with natural springs in this area.

name: Zarzaquemada
etymology_summary: Named after the Zarzaquemada barrio of Leganes, the most densely populated district. 'Zarza' = bramble/blackberry bush; 'quemada' = burnt. The name likely refers to the historical practice of burning brambles to clear land for cultivation or settlement.

name: Villalba
etymology_summary: Named after Collado Villalba municipality. 'Collado' = mountain pass; 'Villalba' from Latin 'villa alba' (white village/estate). Major railway junction where lines to Segovia, Avila, and the Sierra diverge.

name: Las Zorreras
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Zorreras area near El Escorial. 'Zorreras' derives from 'zorra' (fox), meaning 'place of foxes'. References the historically abundant fox population in the wooded Sierra foothills.

name: Zarzalejo
etymology_summary: Named after the Zarzalejo municipality. 'Zarzalejo' is a diminutive of 'zarzal' (bramble patch), from 'zarza' (bramble/blackberry bush). Literally 'small bramble patch'. Similar formation to other phytonymic toponyms like Moraleja, Carrascalejo.
